hints: Start from the name PVC, which is poly(chloroethene), and think about what its single monomer looks like.
The monomer is $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCl}$, so after addition polymerisation the repeat unit must be $-\text{CH}_2-\text{CHCl}-$.
Look for the chain where $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CHCl}$ groups strictly alternate, giving one Cl on every other carbon.
walkthrough:
**Recall the monomer for PVC**

PVC stands for polyvinyl chloride, which is systematically poly(chloroethene). Its monomer is chloroethene.

$$\text{CH}_2 = \text{CHCl}$$

**Work out the repeat unit**

In addition polymerisation the C=C double bond opens to form two new C-C single bonds to neighbours. Each monomer therefore becomes:

$$-\text{CH}_2-\text{CHCl}-$$

**Check the pattern in the chain**

This means a correct section must show strict alternation. One carbon has 2 H atoms ($-\text{CH}_2-$), the next has 1 H and 1 Cl ($-\text{CHCl}-$), then repeat. That gives exactly one Cl on every second carbon atom, which matches only one of the diagrams.

options.A: Shows perfect alternation of $-\text{CH}_2-$ and $-\text{CHCl}-$. Reading left to right: $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CHCl}$, $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CHCl}$, $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CHCl}$. There is one Cl on every other carbon, exactly the repeat unit of poly(chloroethene).
options.B: Shows a Cl on every carbon, so every unit is $-\text{CHCl}-$. This would come from polymerising 1,2-dichloroethene, $\text{CHCl}=\text{CHCl}$, not chloroethene. Students choose this by thinking every carbon in PVC must carry Cl.
options.C: Shows Cl atoms only on carbons 2 and 6, with long runs of $-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-$ in between. Addition polymers have a regular repeating unit, not random spacing of substituents. This is a trap for not checking the whole chain.
options.D: Also shows a Cl on every carbon, with each carbon as $-\text{CHCl}-$. This is the same composition as B (just drawn with all Cl on top) and corresponds to poly(dichloroethene), not PVC where only half the carbons carry Cl.
